title: Sixty galaxy clusters become cosmic magnifying glasses for JWST
freshness: Preprint first submitted 5 November 2026; within the 15-day search window; not yet peer reviewed.
excerpt: Galaxy clusters bend and amplify light from much more distant objects. A new JWST-assisted study maps 60 of these natural telescopes using thousands of repeated images.
whyItMatters: More reliable cluster mass maps help astronomers estimate the true brightness of extremely distant galaxies and select targets for early-universe studies.

exploreFurther.label: VENUS: Strong Lens Mass Models and Einstein Radii of 60 Galaxy Clusters (preprint)

whatToExploreNext: How do multiple images of one galaxy reveal the distribution of invisible mass in a foreground cluster?
body:
## A telescope gets help from gravity

Some of the universe's best telescopes are not machines. They are enormous groups of galaxies whose gravity bends light from objects much farther away. A new study has mapped 60 of these natural magnifying glasses, giving astronomers a better way to search for faint galaxies in the early universe.

The project is called VENUS, short for Vast Exploration for Nascent, Unexplored Sources. Its team used observations from the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) to refine models of the mass inside 60 galaxy clusters. The study was submitted as a preprint on November 5, 2026 and has not yet undergone peer review.

## Why a galaxy cluster can magnify light

Einstein's theory of gravity predicts that mass bends the path of light. A galaxy cluster contains galaxies, gas, and large quantities of invisible dark matter. Together they distort the light from galaxies behind the cluster. Astronomers call this gravitational lensing.

A distant galaxy can appear as a stretched arc, a brightened patch, or several images of the same object. These multiple images are especially useful. If researchers know which patches came from one background galaxy, they can adjust a model of the foreground cluster until the predicted positions match the observations.

The result is a map of how the cluster bends light. It can tell observers where to look for background galaxies too faint to see without the cluster's help. But a lens is not a perfect glass magnifier: its distortion varies from place to place, and inferred brightness depends on the accuracy of the mass model.

## Thousands of clues in sixty clusters

The VENUS researchers fitted the positions of approximately 4,500 multiple images across the 60 clusters. Around 1,150 of those images were newly identified with help from JWST's observations in several wavelength bands.

They used software called glafic to build mass models and checked their robustness with a jackknife procedure, a method that repeats an analysis while leaving out subsets of the data. This helps reveal whether a result depends too strongly on particular observations.

One measure of a cluster's lensing strength is its Einstein radius, an angular scale associated with especially strong light bending. For a hypothetical background source at redshift nine, the median radius in this selected sample was about 30 arcseconds. Some clusters reached roughly 60 arcseconds. Redshift nine refers to an era when the universe was only a small fraction of its current age.

Three clusters stood out for especially large Einstein radii and areas of strong magnification: MACS J0717.5+3745, MACS J0600.1-2008, and PLCK G287.0+32.9.

## What the maps can and cannot tell us

These clusters were selected because they are powerful lenses. Their large magnification is therefore not representative of galaxy clusters in general. The team's measured Einstein radii were compatible with predictions from the standard cold dark matter picture. That agreement does not directly detect dark matter or prove that model uniquely correct.

The practical payoff is a better set of gravitational maps. JWST can use them to estimate the intrinsic brightness and size of distant sources, and to choose promising regions for future observations. A faint smudge behind a cluster may be a galaxy that formed when the cosmos was young. Understanding the foreground lens is what lets astronomers reconstruct that distant galaxy more reliably.

**Measured:** positions of multiple lensed images and the resulting angular lensing scales. **Inferred:** the clusters' mass distributions and magnifications of background galaxies.
